summary:
Onur Solmaz introduces himself as a founding engineer who has built AI coding harnesses since before ChatGPT, starting with a JupyterLab extension over the original Codex DaVinci Code 2 model. He became an OpenClaw maintainer after being impressed by Peter's early Claude work and the Claude Bot in Discord. His focus is now on agent interoperability and orchestration, aiming to accelerate enterprise adoption.

He describes "Discord-driven development" — running one to five parallel Codex sessions through Discord channels, each bound to a task. This led to building acpx, a headless CLI for the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). ACP standardizes agent-to-client interaction, distinct from MCP which gives tools to the model. acpx functions as a Swiss Army knife for ACP, allowing any agent to call any other agent over the command line.

OpenClaw faces enormous scale: over 60K total PRs, 300–500 per day, most AI-generated and not mergeable. Each PR is signal about something broken. Onur built an abstract workflow engine — described as A10-like — that drives Codex sessions through nodes: find intent, judge implementation, check conflicts, run review-refactor loops, make CI pass, and emit structured JSON. He argues that running agents in loops for shallow bug discovery and superficial refactors is acceptable, while fundamental refactors should be escalated to humans.

He envisions on-demand disposable agents — one agent per task, fully synchronized, with per-task compute environments. This requires Kubernetes, an agent harness (OpenClaw, Codex, Cloud Code, or ACP), read-write access, and state synchronization via rsync or Dropbox-like algorithms. A key limitation is that current chat platforms (Slack, Teams, Discord) don't support multi-agent provisioning; you must manually create separate app manifests per agent. Enterprise agents will consume far more inference than personal agents, making enterprise the bigger market.

The talk concludes with Onur's work at TextCortex (explicitly distinct from OpenClaw): an open-source Kubernetes orchestrator with a Go operator that provisions a full compute environment per task. The demo shows dispatching agents for error reporting on Slack after prod releases — users ask a concierge agent to debug, and a new agent is spawned in a web UI (a React app hosted in the cluster) since agents can't be placed directly into Slack. Agents run in full Kubernetes pods — wasteful but a better abstraction, as OpenClaw showed the power of giving agents full computers. OpenHands uses Firecracker for virtualization; Onur notes he is still learning about different virtualization frameworks. The system is built on ACP, making it agent-agnostic, and Onur offers to help open-source projects set it up for processing hundreds of issues per day.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Background and OpenClaw Journey
sections.summary: Onur introduces his background: building AI coding harnesses since before ChatGPT, starting with a JupyterLab extension over Codex DaVinci Code 2. He became an OpenClaw maintainer after being impressed by Peter's early Claude work. His focus is now agent interoperability and orchestration, with a goal of accelerating enterprise adoption.

sections.title: Discord-Driven Development and ACPX Introduction
sections.summary: Onur describes running 1–5 parallel Codex sessions from Discord channels, binding channels to Codex through ACP. He demonstrates using ACPX to convert ACP docs to PDF before flying to London. He notes that Codex cannot send files back through Discord directly, requiring channel switching.

sections.title: ACP vs MCP and the Protocol Landscape
sections.summary: Onur clarifies ACP standardizes agent-to-client interaction, while MCP provides tools to the model. He chose ACP because it had adapters for Codex and Claude Code when needed. Competing agent-to-agent protocols exist; long-term OpenClaw will support all. ACPX started as a CLI for calling any agent over the command line and is becoming a Swiss Army knife for ACP.

sections.title: OpenClaw PR Scale and Workflow Automation
sections.summary: OpenClaw faces 60K+ total PRs, 300–500 per day, most AI-generated and not mergeable. Each PR is signal about something broken. Onur built an A10-like workflow engine driving Codex sessions through nodes: find intent, judge implementation, check conflicts, run review-refactor loops, make CI pass, emit structured JSON. He argues loops for shallow bugs are fine; fundamental refactors go to humans.

sections.title: On-Demand Disposable Agents Vision
sections.summary: Onur envisions one disposable agent per task, fully synchronized, with per-task compute environments. Enterprise agents will consume more inference than personal ones, making enterprise the bigger market. Current chat platforms lack multi-agent provisioning support — you must manually create separate app manifests per agent, which must change for the vision to work.

sections.title: Kubernetes Orchestrator and TextCortex Demo
sections.summary: Onur presents his TextCortex work (explicitly separate from OpenClaw): an open-source Kubernetes orchestrator with a Go operator that provisions full compute environments per task. It requires Kubernetes, an agent harness, read-write access, and state synchronization (rsync or Dropbox-like algorithms). The demo shows Slack error reporting — a concierge agent dispatches new agents to debug bugs after prod releases. Agents can't be placed directly into Slack, so a React web UI hosted in the cluster handles conversations. Each agent runs in a full Kubernetes pod — wasteful but a better abstraction, echoing OpenClaw's philosophy of giving agents full computers. OpenHands uses Firecracker for virtualization; Onur is still learning about frameworks. The system is agent-agnostic via ACP. He offers to help open-source projects set it up for processing hundreds of issues per day.
